title: 2 Kings 15:32–38
context: In Judah, Jotham son of Uzziah reigns sixteen years. He does what is right, as his father did, though the high places remain, and he builds the upper gate of the LORD's house. In his days the LORD begins to send Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel against Judah, setting the stage for the crisis under Ahaz.

verses.text: In the second year of Pekah the son of Remaliah king of Israel, Jotham the son of Uzziah king of Judah began to reign.
verses.arminianNotes: Jotham begins to reign in the second year of Pekah. Arminian readers note that his reign overlaps with Israel's decline, giving Judah a clear example of where unfaithfulness leads.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jotham had already governed for his father (15:5). His formal reign continues a period of relative faithfulness in Judah while Israel falls apart.

verses.text: He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jerusha the daughter of Zadok.
verses.arminianNotes: He is twenty-five at his accession and reigns sixteen years; his mother is Jerusha daughter of Zadok. Arminian readers note the opportunity of a long reign to lead Judah toward God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the regnal details follow the standard pattern for Judah's kings. The name of each king's mother is consistently recorded in the Judean notices.

verses.text: He did that which was right in the LORD’s eyes. He did according to all that his father Uzziah had done.
verses.arminianNotes: He does what is right, as Uzziah did. Arminian readers note that he follows his father's good example, a reminder of how faithful parents can shape the next generation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Chronicles 27:6 adds, "Jotham became mighty, because he ordered his ways before the LORD his God." His strength is credited to his walk with God.

verses.text: However the high places were not taken away. The people still sacrificed and burned incense in the high places. He built the upper gate of the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: The high places remain, but he builds the upper gate of the LORD's house. Arminian readers see a king investing in the temple while leaving the popular high places untouched.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the refrain about the high places recurs. Jotham's building work honors the temple, yet the nation's worship remains divided and incomplete.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Jotham, and all that he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of Jotham's acts are in the chronicles of the kings of Judah. Arminian readers note that his reign is summarized briefly, with his faithfulness and building work highlighted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the standard closing formula. Second Chronicles 27 gives fuller detail, but Kings focuses on the covenant verdict and the threat that follows.

verses.text: In those days, the LORD began to send Rezin the king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah against Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: "The LORD began to send Rezin the king of Syria and Pekah" against Judah. Arminian readers note that God works through the free actions of nations to discipline and warn his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the narrator credits the LORD with sending these enemies. God governs the movements of nations, using them to accomplish his purposes in Judah's history.

verses.text: Jotham slept with his fathers, and was buried with his fathers in his father David’s city; and Ahaz his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Jotham is buried in David's city, and Ahaz succeeds him. Arminian readers note that a faithful father does not guarantee a faithful son, as the next chapter will sadly show.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the transition to Ahaz brings a sharp turn in Judah's story. God's covenant with David continues, even as Ahaz departs from David's way.
